sources.title: NGSS MS-ESS1-1: Develop and use a model of the Earth-sun-moon system to describe the cyclic patterns of lunar phases, eclipses of the sun and moon, and seasons
OpenStax Astronomy 2e, 4.7 Eclipses of the Sun and Moon

legend.name: Eclipsed moon
legend.meaning: A full moon in Earth's shadow glows dull coppery red

steps.title: Sun
steps.instruction: Trace the sun in the top picture.

note.text: Any solid object in sunlight casts a shadow into space behind it. An eclipse happens when that shadow falls on another body.

steps.title: Moon
steps.instruction: Trace the moon between the sun and Earth.

note.text: The moon is between the sun and Earth, so it's at new moon phase.
The sun is about 400 times wider than the moon, but also about 400 times farther away, so they look the same size.

steps.title: Moon's shadow
steps.instruction: Draw the moon's dark shadow narrowing to a point on Earth.

note.text: Where this darkest shadow, the umbra, touches Earth, the moon hides the sun: a total solar eclipse.

steps.title: Sun
steps.instruction: Trace the sun in the bottom picture.

note.text: Now the order changes: sun, then Earth, then moon.

steps.title: Earth
steps.instruction: Trace Earth between the sun and the moon.

note.text: Earth is bigger than the moon, so its shadow is much bigger and longer.

steps.title: Earth's shadow
steps.instruction: Draw the two edges of Earth's shadow.

note.text: Earth's shadow stretches far out into space, away from the sun.

steps.title: Moon
steps.instruction: Trace the moon inside Earth's shadow.

note.text: The moon is opposite the sun, at full moon, and passes into Earth's shadow: a lunar eclipse.

steps.title: Lunar eclipse color
steps.question: Why does the moon glow dull red, not go fully black, in a total lunar eclipse?

options.text: Sunlight bends through Earth's atmosphere into the shadow
options.feedback: Yes. A little sunlight passes through our air and is bent into Earth's shadow, lighting the moon a coppery red.

options.text: The moon makes its own red light
options.feedback: The moon makes no light. The red is sunlight bent through Earth's atmosphere.
Mars is far too faint. The glow is sunlight bent through Earth's atmosphere.
It's not heat. Sunlight passing through our atmosphere bends into the shadow.

steps.title: Not every month
steps.instruction: The moon passes new and full every month.
steps.question: Why don't we get a solar and a lunar eclipse every month?

options.text: The moon's orbit is tilted about 5°, so it usually passes above or below the shadows
options.feedback: Right. Eclipses happen only when the sun, Earth and moon line up exactly, during eclipse seasons twice a year.

options.text: The moon stops moving some months
options.feedback: The moon always orbits. Its tilted orbit usually carries it above or below the line.

options.text: The sun is too far away
options.feedback: Distance stays about the same. The tilt of the moon's orbit is what matters.
Eclipses can happen at any time of year, whenever the sun, Earth and moon line up.

steps.title: Who sees it?
steps.question: Why do far more people see a total lunar eclipse than a total solar eclipse?

options.text: A lunar eclipse is visible from Earth's whole night side; the moon's umbra covers only a thin path
options.feedback: Yes. Anyone who can see the full moon sees it darken, but only people in the umbra's narrow path see the sun fully hidden.

options.text: Lunar eclipses happen in the daytime
options.feedback: Lunar eclipses happen at night, at full moon, for everyone on the night side.

options.text: The sun is bigger than Earth
options.feedback: True, but the reason is shadow size: the moon's umbra only touches a small patch of Earth.

options.text: Solar eclipses are too dim to see
options.feedback: They're dramatic, but visible only in the narrow path where the umbra lands.
